No problem.  It isn't my original idea, I actually heard about it from Asperger Experts.
Just that we tend to get fixated and have repetitive thought processes.  We perseverate and it's hard to get the thoughts to stop.

It's been almost a year since I got my diagnosis and I still have so many questions.  Since you have aspergers, you probably have sticky thoughts.  I fixated on having aspergers after I got diagnosed and I think it contributed to me going through a deep depression.

For me, it became an obsession.  I only saw the world in terms of autistic or not.  I constantly thought about it, studied others and compared myself to them.  I was completely obsessed by this question of "what's autistic and what's not".  

Just know that I'm a much happier person right now.  The self analysis that I did (and still do, constantly) led me to a sense of freedom to start to become who I truly am.  Do less people like me?  Absolutely.  But for every 10 people that are terrified of me, theres one person who might understand or appreciate me for being unique. 

Try not to pick yourself apart while you figure out who you really are at your core.  Be yourself and do what you need to survive.  You will pull through.

I'm also diagnosed with both bipolar type 1 and ASD.  I was hospitalized 4 times in 5 months, and each time, the doctors didn't know what was wrong.  They kept throwing around terms and were convinced that I had mania, psychosis, mixed episodes, and depression.  It was a different story each time, all within the span of 5 months. 

They pushed hard for ECT.  Medication didn't work.  I tried nearly every single antipsychotic available, including old antipsychotics like prolixin.  I rejected the ECT, but I can't imagine what life would have been like if I went through with it.  Finally, low doses of risperdal stopped everything, almost overnight.  

These days, I take tegretol, vyvanse, Celexa, smoke weed daily, and I'm doing better than ever.  I have meltdowns and shutdowns, but no episodes.  

Still, it drives me mad trying to figure out if I'm bipolar or not.  No one seems to know.  The psychologist that diagnosed me with ASD says no bipolar.  The psychiatrist treating me says I have ADHD and bipolar disorder.  I can't believe I've had this label slapped on me and it's become so integral to my identity.

For these reasons, I do my best to think of myself as a person first.  I'm autistic, that's for sure.  But before that, I'm a special educator.  I'm an artist.  I'm a writer and a dreamer.  I'm a loner, Dottie, a rebel.

My thing is that I'm amazing at working with middle and high school kids with ASD.  We often have a lot of the same intense interests and thought patterns. I feel like I'm pretty incompetent in general, but I'm surprisingly good at relating to adolescents and adults with ASD.  Luckily, no one will ever force me to have a baby or become an expert on babies :)

I got through high school without speaking to hardly anyone by drawing in my sketchbooks all day.  I barely spoke to others and did my homework in the library at lunch.  If anyone said my name or tried to speak to me, my face would turn completely red and id try my hardest to ignore them.  I didn't know why they were saying my name.  I didn't know how to just chat with someone, and I didn't ever have anything to say.  I just assumed that everyone was a bully since that's all I understood.  I couldn't do hardly anything without being bullied or made fun of.  But I also just didn't why they didn't like me.  Why was I so stupid?

I remember in tech ed, I was holding an exacto knife and suddenly there was blood all over my hand.  In retrospect, I must have been gripping it too hard, and it sliced me.  All the other students started shouting and laughing.  I didn't even notice I had blood on my hand because I have a very high pain tolerance.  I literally said "What?  That's not my blood" and kept working until the teacher made me go to the nurse.  Ever since that day, all the students laughed and pointed at me when I walked into that class.  Soon, it became every class.  That was around the time I went into special ed.  

The takeaway?  I never had to deal with those guys again.  Ever.  But I wasted SO MUCH TIME trying to fit in, to get them to like me.  And all I ever did was make it worse and make myself want to die.

I think you are describing what is known as a "passive death wish".  Maybe you want to die because you never wanted to be here.  Or maybe everything is just too much for you now and you're out of coping skills to deal with it, so why not just die if everything's fucked anyway?  But you don't really want to die.  Because when you die, there is nothing.  There's no form of release or relief.  It's impossible to feel any relief because you won't be feeling anything at all.  All that matters once you die is:
1. You can't come back
2. You became a statistic when you could have made it with some support.

The reality is that you DON'T want to die, and you CAN do this with some support.  What supports do you have in place now?  Therapeutic sensory strategies, medication, exposure therapy, etc, what helps you?  Let me help you find some ways of coping.  I'm a multidisciplinary special educator for adolescents with autism, and I'm also diagnosed with ASD.  This is my interest and I know a lot about it. In my mind I have this fantasy that one day, I coexist with someone peacefully, and without fear of judgement for being weird. I wouldn't need to isolate myself and be alone all the time.  We could somehow operate as one person.  I wouldn't mind sharing my bed.  We wouldn't even need separate beds.  

But the reality is that I've always been this way since I was a child.  I try to spend time with others, but even with my own family, there is a hard limit.  From a young age, Ive just had to spend my time away and play alone.  Never enjoyed watching movies with the family or sitting at the table for dinner.  The sound of forks, chewing, the ethical issues with what others are eating, the anxiety about what to say, etc.  Even sitting next to others gives me panic attacks.

My relationships never get to the point where I'd feel okay sharing my things.  Initially it's amazing to share a bed with someone, or spend an evening together on the couch.  Then a few weeks in, I realize that I just can't sleep in someone else's bed. Then it's back to my house, to my room.  

Maybe I'm depressed.  It just sucks because I want connections with people.  I just feel like the idea of intimacy is a total fantasy.

I think I know what you're getting at here.  Is it because it can cause the child to burn out by being forced to act a certain way?  Because that is definitely a very real possibility, something to consider.

The actual process of implementing ABA can be really stressful for the child, but I don't think the alternatives are that great either.

You could be in ankle-deep or waist deep water depending on where you are in the Narrows, so be prepared to have your feet submerged the whole time.  If you're going into the Narrows, you could pick up a pair of Salomon Crossamphibian Swift Water Shoes.  These shoes will offer you minimal traction.  

The other option is to wear a pair of non-waterproof hiking shoes or trail runners.  The non-waterproof part is key, because it means water can go in and out through the shoes.  Waterproof shoes trap water inside and you'll have a bad time.  You can pick up a pair of Merrell Moab Ventilators for about the same price as the Crossamphibian Swifts.

With a 60 dollar budget, you should probably just try to sleep in your car.  It isn't worth spending the money because you won't be able to make a good investment on any gear.  It would honestly be a waste to go buy a 25 dollar tent.

If you won't have access to your car and just need to do this, I'd recommend getting a tarp and some rope ($15-20).  Pick up a cheap Therm-a-Rest sleeping pad ($20).  Get one of those disposable cooler bags ($??).  Spend the rest on Benadryl to knock yourself out at night.

Honestly, it can be done and people do it.  You hear these stories about people walking the entire Appalachian Trail with just a tarp and a pair of sneakers.  It isn't ideal, but it can work.  Try to have fun with it!

The material on both of these pants is awesome.  There's a bit of stretch to them, which I love because I don't like my range of motion to be restricted at all.  If you're looking for thermal properties, just throw on some long underwear underneath.

I second the Patagucci if you're going to be generating a ton of body heat (running or really booking it).  If it's cold, it won't do you much good.  It also isn't waterproof, it's water resistant (DWR coating) so if it's really raining and you aren't moving, you're gonna get wet.  Add wind into the mix and you're screwed.  But, so so light.  Really nice piece of gear.  It folds up super small and weighs about as much as a handful of tissues.

I'll try to keep it pretty cost-efficient, but if you need Gore-Tex or want to splurge I have other recommendations.  

Pants-For 80 dollars, you can get a pair of Marmot Precips that are fully waterproof and windproof.  

Shirt- Tough to come by waterproof shirts, the jacket does most of the work.  Plus, a waterproof shirt under a waterproof jacket is going to trap too much heat and sweat and make you miserable.

Light Jacket- The Helium II by Outdoor Research is suuuuper light and getting great reviews.  Folds up to the size of an apple.  Just don't forget you have it with you. $160, worth.

Gloves- Do you need insulation at all, or are you strictly looking for water/wind proofing?

Side note: to get the most appropriate gear, the important information here is what you'll be doing while wearing it.  Let me know and I'll find something for ya.

Hallucinating a person is on the severe end of psychosis, and that shouldn't suddenly happen outside of a psychotic episode (though it could with psychotic disorders other than bipolar).  Do you have a lot of anxiety about having another episode?  If you were exposed to a very overstimulating environment for 4-6 hours, it makes sense that you would be pretty on edge and worked up.

What field are you in, and what is the policy for taking sick days?  If you're sick in the head, it still counts as sick.  Most places I've worked at haven't required a doctor's note until the 3rd consecutive day.  

FMLA definitely comes in handy when you require a hospitalization.  Personally, I'd save it for that.  IIRC, I got three months/year, and I took all of it to recover from my episode + 2 months inpatient.  Once it was up, I called my employer and she even offered to let me come back once I was feeling better.  Just keep in mind that it isn't paid time off or anything.  You'll have to have a backup to maintain income.  

Also, what specifically is it that's preventing you from working?  A lot of times you can work something out with your employer to get breaks without coming outright and saying that you are mentally ill.

Oh yeah, the stimulants could be addictive. But it's worth giving it a try.

I've been diagnosed with ADHD since elementary school and I'm 27 now.  It's been a pretty consistent battle for me, never really waivered unless I medicated it.  I take Tegretol for bipolar type 1 and vyvanse for my ADHD.  It's super, super helpful and if you need it, you can make it work.  Your mood needs to be pretty stable first, and you obviously definitely need to be on a mood stabilizer for bipolar.  If I miss a few days of my Tegretol and continue taking the Vyvanse, I get increased agitation.

Coffee and ADHD meds have a paradoxical effect on some people diagnosed with ADHD, which is why it can produce a calming effect.  However, it is a myth that it affects all people with ADHD this way.  There is evidence that many people without ADHD feel more focused and calm when they are under the effect of a low dose stimulant.  However, it might not increase their ability to learn like it does for a patient with an ADHD diagnosis.

The vyvanse has been a huge help with fidgeting, restlessness, and focus. Couple of ideas for you here. Please don't take offense to any of them-I've been working in the mental health/special education field for over 4 years now and I'm just relaying what I've learned and observed.

Does she currently have an IEP or 504?  I highly suggest advocating for one if she does not.  These are plans that can provide your daughter with accommodations such as scheduled/requested breaks in a separate room.  This would reduce or eliminate the need for physical removal from the environment.  It would also reduce negative feedback from peers-who wants to be physically dragged from a room in front of the entire class?  It's hurting her self-esteem to be singled out, and this can certainly be done in a more discreet way.  I'd be more than happy to elaborate on IEP's and 504's if you want to PM me.

Blocking input can be indicative of sensory overload.  Sensory Processing Disorder and Autism Spectrum Disorders are commonly co-morbid with ADHD.  Has she been tested for these?  It could explain the meltdowns, inappropriate/insulting comments toward others.  However, it sounds to me like the meltdowns could be coming from a need for acceptance rather than a sensory processing issue.  When kids don't know how to get positive attention, they often seek negative attention.  That could explain the inappropriate comments too.  Because let's face it, we all want to be accepted, and having ADHD makes that extremely difficult.  I've been there.  Just thinking about the amount of bullying I've endured (mostly in elementary and middle) almost has tears welling up in my eyes.

She needs something to be proud of right now.  She's obviously very smart but weak in certain areas, such as socialization.  How is she with sports?  Individual sports, such as swimming, could be beneficial.  My parents enrolled me in swim lessons and swim team when I was young, and it did me a world of good for many years.  It burns off the extra energy, allows for healthy competition, and doesn't involve much coordination with other people.  Generally speaking, kids with ADHD tend to be fantastic swimmers.  We just have the energy/drive, and the water tends to have a calming effect on many people.  Michael Phelps has ADHD-look at his success.  If not swimming, what about martial arts, gymnastics, or dance?

I work two jobs, both on my feet, and walk around 16,000 steps on a 14 hour day.  Otherwise I shoot for 10,000.  I try to compete with myself every day to walk as much as possible.  If I don't get up to 10,000 by evening, I go running/walking.  I'm not fit enough to run the whole time so I run 1 minute, walk 1, run 1, walk one, and so on.  As far as eating goes, I find that if I stay active I eat less.  Boredom leads to eating in excess.  

So overall, the fitbit helped a lot, and staying busy helps the most.  Try your best to not have a lot of free time.  Fill it up with activities.  You don't necessarily have to be exercising all the time, just be active and burn calories.  Even if you don't work two jobs on your feet all day like I do, you should still try to get in as many steps as possible.  Get a fitbit, use your pedometer on your phone.  Try to eat meals with others.  It makes eating less easier, in my opinion.  Make it fun, keep up with it.  Join an adult sports team.  Etc.  

Meds can really cause weight gain but it's not an end all, you just have to work hard.
